notes: Spending is net revenue spending on waste collection, disposal, recycling and waste minimisation, plus the waste levy paid to joint disposal authorities. Trade (business) waste and street cleaning are excluded.
Recycling rates are driven by what a council collects (separate food waste, garden waste charges, how bins are collected) as much as by how much it spends.
District councils only collect; the county council disposes of what is collected, so their spending and results describe collection only.

notes: Spending adds revenue spending on structural and routine maintenance of roads and bridges to capital spending on roads, street lighting and road safety, averaged over three years, per kilometre of road the council manages (DfT road length statistics).
Capital spending includes new roads, street lighting and safety schemes as well as resurfacing, and councils are also paid for roads by central government: the match is rough.
Condition comes from machine surveys (SCANNER) reported to the nearest whole per cent, averaged over the last three years. Heavy-traffic and urban roads wear faster than quiet rural ones.

notes: Spending is the Treasury's Education function for the whole UK at every level (early years to universities, including student support), in 2025-26 prices, divided by state-funded school pupils in England: a trend indicator, not what a school receives per pupil.

Key stage 2 tests were not held in 2019-20 and 2020-21. GCSE and A level grades in 2019-20 and 2020-21 were set by teachers, and 2021-22 grading was deliberately generous as results moved back towards normal, so those years are not comparable.
Attainment 8 and the 9 to 1 GCSE grades were phased in from 2016-17; earlier years are not comparable and are omitted.
School results depend on far more than spending: pupil intake, teacher supply, curriculum and exam changes, and the pandemic.

Spending is the Treasury's Health function for the whole UK (in 2025-26 prices); the waiting list is for England only. Health spending in England is about 85% of the UK total and the two have moved together, but this is a trend indicator rather than a like-for-like ratio.
The waiting list counts pathways (referrals), not people: the same patient can be on it more than once. The figures use NHS England's estimates for trusts that did not report (England-wide totals).
Waiting times are for consultant-led treatment only. The list is affected by activity in primary care, social care (delayed discharges), staffing and strikes, as well as by spending.
From February 2024 community service pathways stopped being counted, which lowered the list slightly; earlier months are not restated.
